claims.text: Homogenized Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a single BCC phase at high temperature.
Phase stability during cooling and thermal exposure is governed by partitioning of Al and Cr between BCC and FCC regions.
Al and Cr partitioning drives formation of a two-phase BCC-FCC microstructure.
The BCC-FCC microstructure forms through spinodal decomposition.
The degree of chemical partitioning and the resulting phase fractions depend on cooling rate.
Slower cooling permits greater chemical partitioning and coarsening.
Greater partitioning and coarsening during slow cooling produce more distinct BCC and FCC regions.
Rapid quenching suppresses chemical partitioning and retains a more homogeneous BCC structure.
Local composition fluctuations and differential solute partitioning, especially involving Al and Cr, drive phase separation.
FCC regions may form from the BCC matrix by nucleation and growth rather than spinodal decomposition.
Slower cooling and/or annealing increases the prominence of BCC-FCC phase separation and Al/Cr partitioning.
The fraction and size of FCC regions increase with slower cooling and longer annealing.
A rapidly quenched baseline should remain mostly single-phase BCC with minimal chemical partitioning.
Phase separation will not occur when cooling is fast enough to freeze atomic mobility.
The proposed mechanism may not apply after a significant reduction in the alloy's Al or Cr content.
The proposed mechanism also applies to similar high-entropy alloys with comparable composition and an initial BCC state.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis specifically attributes two-phase formation to spinodal decomposition, whereas the mechanism permits either spinodal decomposition or nucleation and growth, and the uncertainty field states that these alternatives are not distinguished.
